name: Grigorios Chrysos
talk: Are activation functions required for learning in all deep networks?
abstract: Activation functions play a pivotal role in deep neural networks, enabling them to tackle complex tasks like image recognition. However, activation functions also introduce significant challenges for deep learning theory, network dynamics analysis, and properties such as interpretability and privacy preservation. In this talk, we revisit the necessity of activation functions across various scenarios. Specifically, we explore expressing network outputs through high-order interactions among input elements using multilinear algebra. Interestingly, tensors emerge naturally in this scenario and enable us certain flexibility in determining what types of interactions we want and how they are captured. Now, the question becomes: Are tensors alone sufficient for effective learning (e.g. in ImageNet-level recognition)?

name: Xiao Fu
abstract:
Tensor signal processing has a long history in applications such as wireless channel estimation, array processing, hyperspectral imaging, and audio source separation. Since the 1990s, the signal processing community has pioneered the use of tensor models by representing multidimensional data as low-rank tensors and exploiting their unique structural properties, particularly the identifiability of tensor decompositions. Recent advances in generative AI have created new opportunities for sensing, communication, and imaging by enabling the learning of highly expressive data representations through neural models. However, applying these methods directly to tensor-valued data remains challenging. The high dimensionality and complex structure of tensors often lead to substantial computational costs, large model sizes, and increased training data requirements.

In this talk, we share our experience in integrating tensor signal processing principles with modern generative AI. Our observations are threefold: (1) tensor-valued signals can benefit significantly from the expressive modeling power of generative models for tasks such as sensing, reconstruction, and super-resolution; (2) the physical and mathematical structures underlying tensor signals—especially low-rank decomposition structures and the identifiability of their latent factors—can often substantially reduce the modeling burden of generative AI; and (3) combining identifiable tensor representations with factorized generative modeling often yields an attractive balance among efficiency, interpretability, and performance. We illustrate these ideas through recent work on radio map-based environment sensing and hyperspectral image super-resolution. More broadly, we believe that the greatest opportunities in next-generation tensor signal processing systems may lie not in applying generative AI to tensor data in a black-box fashion, but in carefully integrating generative models with the underlying structures of tensor signals.
